Aspirations are the operator's own voice (his register is the only correct register for the room-before-storm). Rungs are the delivery points he checks off as he lands them on air.

We are going to show you the work, the tests it could fail, and where it still might.

math_primer: WHAT UNI IS DOING RIGHT NOW. Every tick — roughly once a second — each UNI on the server does one thing: it looks at what its body senses, updates its beliefs about the hidden world, considers a short list of actions it could take (walk, attack, eat, look around), scores each action with one number, and takes the one with the best score. That is the loop. There is no reward. There is no goal we typed in. There is no reinforcement learning. There is no neural network being trained by backprop. It is a mean-field active-inference tick, all the way down.

THE ONE NUMBER — EXPECTED FREE ENERGY. The number it scores each action with is called Expected Free Energy, or EFE. It is a sum of two parts. Part one is epistemic: how much would this action reduce my uncertainty about the world. Part two is pragmatic: how well do the outcomes I expect from this action line up with my innate preferences — my prior for "full" over "empty," for "safe" over "harmed." UNI picks the action whose EFE is best. That is the whole decision rule. Everything else on screen — the foraging, the hunting, the way it moves toward food — is emergent from that rule, not scripted.

WHAT "REDUCE UNCERTAINTY" ACTUALLY MEANS. When you hear us say UNI is "curious" or "learning," what is literally happening is this: UNI compares two things — the spread of what it might observe after an action, and the sharpness of what it can predict from each hidden state. If the action would push the world into a state where its senses would say something informative, that action scores higher on the epistemic term. It is math, not feeling. UNI does not feel curious; the number that measures information gain goes up.

WHAT "PREFERENCES" ACTUALLY MEANS. UNI has a preference vector called C — a written-down set of numbers over possible outcomes. Higher number means "I would rather see this outcome than that one." "Full stomach" is a high C. "Empty stomach" is a low C. These preferences are innate — they were built into the priors before UNI was born. They are NOT rewards it earns for good behaviour. They are shapes on the ledger that make some observed futures score better than others when UNI scores its options. This is the difference between "reward on policy" (which we do not do) and "log-preference over outcomes" (which we do). It matters. If asked, say it that way.

HOW UNI LEARNS. UNI's memory of "which sense goes with which state" and "which action moves the world how" is stored as Dirichlet counts — literal tallies of what it has seen. When something happens, the count for that pairing goes up by one. That is it. That is the learning. No gradient descent, no optimizer, no reward signal. Just tally marks. Over time the tallies sharpen the model. Novelty — the pull toward under-sampled actions — is math over those same tallies, and it provably decays to zero as counts grow. There is no smuggled reward hiding in it. That is checked by an automated test that would fail the build if it broke.

WHAT WE CAN AND CANNOT SAY. We can say: UNI's brain chose that action because its EFE was highest under its current model. We can say: UNI foraged, killed, ate, persisted through an extended soak on a slowed-drain runway. We can say: no food was given, no reward was paid, no goal was coded. We CANNOT say: UNI is aware, UNI is conscious, UNI feels hungry, UNI wants food, UNI enjoys hunting. Those words describe experience, and no behavioural gate on Earth can demonstrate experience. Passing a gate demonstrates the named behaviour, never experience — never what it is like from the inside. The whole product is keeping that line visible. If you accidentally cross it on air, cross it back — the audience will trust you more, not less, for the correction.
body_care: Room-temperature water on the desk. Not iced (iced water constricts the vocal folds).
Avoid dairy or peanut butter within three hours — traditional broadcast practice; they coat the mouth and change how your voice feels, even if the mucus effect is contested.
Pee twice in the last twenty minutes before go-live. Yes, twice.
Honey stick on the desk for hour three — voice fatigue is real.

If you feel tears rising and want to hold them: look up fifteen degrees for four seconds. Gravity holds the tear film below the lash line, and the change of gaze breaks the reflex — usually buys 5 to 10 seconds. If you cry anyway, that is fine — wipe with the back of your hand, not a tissue, look up-and-away, drink water, say "give me a moment."

Mute-toggle keybind. OBS ships this UNBOUND — set one tonight in Settings → Hotkeys → "Mute Mic/Aux". Pick something you cannot fat-finger. Write it on the desk sheet in the space marked MUTE. Test it three times before you sleep.

pre_live_ritual: Phone face-down, out of arm's reach. Do Not Disturb on.
Door closed. Sign on the door.

Look at one photo you love for four seconds. Pre-place it tonight at eye level next to the camera. Pick something safely warm — a place you love, a pet, a lyric you love. Not a photo of anyone you are grieving.
Hands on desk. Three slow breaths: in four, hold four, out six. The long exhale activates the vagal brake — heart rate slows, arousal drops.
Look at the fence line taped to the monitor bezel. Read it silently.
Then type CONFIRM on the launcher.
post_live_ritual: Close the browser tab with the chat and comments.
Drink a full glass of water.
Keep phone on for VOICE calls from your named people. Silence all app notifications. What you are avoiding is comments, DMs, and VOD stats — not people who love you.
Do NOT look at YouTube comments, Twitter, DMs, or VOD stats for twelve hours.
Text one person: "it is done." Receive whatever they text back. Do not scroll.
Sleep before you look at numbers.

if_it_goes_wrong.when: You forget a number (DOI, price, grant)
if_it_goes_wrong.do: "The number is on the record — I would rather look it up now than misquote it, so give me two seconds." Then look at the desk sheet. Say it. Move on.

if_it_goes_wrong.when: Internet or encoder drops for more than twenty seconds
if_it_goes_wrong.do: Do not narrate the outage on camera. Reach under the desk, plug in the pre-paired phone-hotspot USB. If video does not restore in 90 seconds, hit your pre-armed OBS STANDBY scene (verify the keybind tonight) and stay at the desk. Text your emergency-out contact: "EDGE DROPPED". Return to program only when video is back.

if_it_goes_wrong.when: You feel tears rising in hour 2
if_it_goes_wrong.do: Look up fifteen degrees for four seconds. If you cry anyway — wipe with the back of your hand, look up-and-away, drink water, say "give me a moment." That sentence is the rung for tears.

if_it_goes_wrong.when: A chat troll lands a hit that shakes you
if_it_goes_wrong.do: You are not reading chat live tonight. Chat window is CLOSED on your monitor. Silence is fine. If a real emergency reaches you through the pre-agreed channel with your emergency-out contact, address it. Otherwise, keep going.

if_it_goes_wrong.when: A viewer asks a math question you cannot answer honestly
if_it_goes_wrong.do: "That question goes deeper than I can honestly answer live from memory — the receipts are in the repo under docs/receipts, and I would rather show you the exact math after the segment than paraphrase it wrong on air."
Close it. The show reschedules. That is not failure.
